text:
Transport budgets are limited, and opinions differ on whether the government should concentrate its money on roads or on public transport. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of roads argue that they remain essential for goods and remote areas. Freight, rural communities and emergency services depend on good roads. A lorry driver who delivers vegetables to a city market, for example, needs wide, well-maintained roads, and no train can reach every village. In countries with scattered populations, public transport is costly and often empty, whereas a good road network gives everyone access to jobs, schools and hospitals. Roads are also needed for buses and taxis, and cars give people freedom to travel at any time. Poorly maintained roads cause accidents and damage vehicles, so repair is a wise use of money.

On the other hand, supporters of public transport argue that it serves more people per unit of space. Trains and buses carry many passengers with less pollution and help those without cars. A tram that carries two hundred passengers, for example, replaces dozens of cars and reduces congestion. Building new roads often encourages more traffic, so they fill again within a few years, whereas improved public transport gives people a real alternative. Cheap and frequent services also help the poor, the young and the elderly to reach work and education, and they reduce greenhouse gases.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that spending should depend on local needs: public transport should come first in large cities, while rural regions need roads that are well maintained.

Phục vụ nhiều người: chở nhiều, ít ô nhiễm; ví dụ xe điện 200 hành khách thay hàng chục xe; đường mới hút xe; lựa chọn thực; giá rẻ giúp người nghèo, trẻ, già; giảm khí nhà kính.
